I'm by no means an expert in weight lifting, but I always hear people talk about "bulking" to get bigger. I'm a thin guy but I want to put on some more muscle mass, but I absolutely do not want to have to get fat to do it. Is bulking a necessary process or can you build muscle while staying thin?

There's so many opinions out there about bulking it's ridiculous. I think as non-professional lifters, bulking/cutting cycles and all that jazz isn't really necessary or applicable for many of us.

You can gain muscle mass without having to gain too much weight but it's a delicate balance of toying with your macros and staying at a caloric deficit. You always want to follow the protein, most people don't really care about the carb/fat ratio too much.

A nice site about lean bulking is from the intermittent fasting guru Martin Berkhan. Go have a look around his blog.

I've been lifting for the past year following my macros and I can tell you that's what's really kept me lean but I still can progress in my lifts. It depends how serious you are about not gaining too much fat. You have to try to shoot for high-protein, low-cal foods in order to reach your daily protein intake but not go too above a certain limit. Check out IIFYM (if it fist your macros) to see how much you need to eat and still progress reasonably in your lifts.

Also a lot is just trial and error. You try a certain caloric goal for a couple of weeks, if it's not giving you the results you want, then make the necessary changes.
Rule 6, keep things on topic. This is not the correct subverse for your question.

Speaking from personal experience...

I went from 5'10" 150 pounds to 5'10" 160 pounds while keeping my body fat around 11-12%. I think if you're near your genetic potential (last 5 or so pounds of muscle you could naturally put on) you might need to bulk. If you're a beginner or intermediate you shouldn't have to put on excess fat to gain muscle - muscle builds painstakingly slow, you only need around a 100-200 calorie per day surplus for muscle growth to occur.

I think bulking and cutting (like most things you find in fitness magazines) is geared towards individuals on steroids, for which it will work very well (but then again, if your on steroids everything works well). For the typical lifter it's not optimal.

TL;DR => You don't need to bulk.

class FileUtils

 attr_accessor :fileName

 def initialize
 @fileName = nil
 end

 def enterFile
 print "Please enter a fileName: "
 fileName = $stdin.gets.chomp
 if !File.file?(fileName)
 puts "File does not exist"
 enterFile
 else
 @fileName = fileName
 puts "File: #{fileName}"
 end
 end
 def deleteFileContents
 open(@fileName, 'w') {|file| file.truncate(0)}
 end
 def addLine
 print "Enter line you would like to add to file: "
 line = $stdin.gets.chomp
 open(@fileName, 'a') { |file| file.puts line }
 end
 def removeLine
 print "What line would you like to remove: "
 lineNumber = $stdin.gets.chomp
 lines = File.readlines(@fileName)
 lines.delete_at(Integer(lineNumber) -1)
 File.open(@fileName, "w+") do |file|
 lines.each { |line| file.puts(line) }
 end
 end
 def viewLines
 File.readlines(@fileName).each { |line| puts line }
 end
end

New to Ruby. Would like some feedback.

Languages like Ruby do not use CamelCase. They use underscores.

As a beginner, it's okay, but I'm interested in the readability of a program and here are a few tips:

When using a ! (not) in an expression, it reads badly: if !File.file?(filename), so I would swap the else around and it reads better. 

if File.file?(filename)
 do something
else
 do something else
end

You could use unless, but I prefer to use unless in statement modifiers only. You don't want readers of your code having to do mental gymnastics.

Use case instead of elsif

DRY up your code: You can do better than these lines.

if ARGV.empty?
 fileUtils.enterFile
else
 if !File.file?(ARGV.first)
 fileUtils.enterFile

Methods should only be doing one thing. printMenu (which should be print_menu or even more professional display_menu) is doing two things. It's displaying the menu and it's reading the response.

You don't need #initialize as you're not initialising anything. @file_name will be nil when it's first encountered.

I'm not going to critique your actual program or what it does as like I said, I like readability.

Obviously I don't know what standard programmer you are, but one of the best books to learn about OO is POODR: Sandi Metz It's a great read, will teach you a lot about Ruby, but more importantly, will teach you how to approach writing an OO program. These tips are transferrable to other languages.

Good luck with your Ruby journey.

edit: As a way of learning to program for one method/class, doing one job, think about writing tests before you write code (Behaviour Driven Development). This way, as you gain in experience, you will easily see that if a test takes a lot to set up, then it's probably wrong. Also, when describing a class or method to someone, if you use the word and in its description, then they're doing too many things. I use RSpec for these sorts of tests (unit) and Cucumber for integration tests.
